title: Where armies camp
hookLine: where armies camp, thorns grow; don't use force (Tao Te Ching 30)

lines: A FIELD AFTER THE SOLDIERS LEAVE.
cards: A field after the soldiers have gone. The tents are packed, the fires are cold, the ground is trampled flat. Nobody plowed this season.
Nobody had the chance. When something finally comes up, it isn't wheat. It's brambles.
Chapter thirty of the Tao Te Ching takes that field and hands it to anyone who stands next to power.
It also closes a week of chapters about not straining: standing on tiptoe, the heavy root, the valley, the vessel you can't seize. Today the same idea meets force head on.

teach.h: ADVICE FOR THE ONE AT THE KING'S ELBOW.
teach.b: First, who the chapter is talking to. In James Legge's translation, it begins with someone who would assist a ruler in harmony with the Tao, and says that person won't assert mastery by force of arms.
It isn't advice for the king. It's advice for the one at the king's elbow. Second, the reason, and the picture.
Force, the chapter says, comes back around on the one who uses it. Then: "Wherever a host is stationed, briars and thorns spring up." A host is an army.
Where it camps, the fields go untended, and what grows is what nobody wanted. Bad years, the chapter adds, follow in the wake of great armies. Force wins the day and sends its bill later.
Third, the chapter doesn't say never act.
It describes a capable leader who strikes when it's truly necessary, gets the result, and stops. No boasting, no pride, no pushing on to prove a point.
And it warns that whatever is driven to the peak of its strength starts to grow old, and that isn't the way of the Tao. Fourth, closer to home. There's no army in the kitchen.
But there are small campaigns: winning the fight about the thermostat, steamrolling a meeting, getting a kid to comply by sheer volume.
Each one can work. The chapter's question is what grows on that ground afterward. A grudge.
A silence. Someone who stops telling you things.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter thirty as advice for anyone near power: do what is necessary, stop there, and remember that force leaves damage behind it.

games.q: you advise a ruler, and a neighbor has crossed a line. the army is ready. what does chapter thirty advise?
o: march in and crush them for good.
do nothing and hope it passes.
games.why: the chapter's capable leader strikes only when it's necessary and stops there, without pride, because force pushed further leaves thorns behind.

practice: Bring to mind one quarrel that's still live, at home, at work, with a neighbor, and notice where you've been pushing. Then ask: what is the smallest thing that actually needs to happen here?
Not winning, just that one thing; hold it, and let the rest of the campaign go quiet.

wordCard.voice: Where armies camp. Chapter thirty's picture: wherever an army is stationed, briars and thorns spring up. Force wins now and leaves the thorns for later. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: no force. The result is enough; the victory lap grows thorns. That's the week.
